answers_by_date.basis: The Convention on the Rights of the Child had constitutional rank under art. 75(22) of the 1994 Constitution and was approved by Ley 23.849 (1990), so the best-interests principle and child-specific protections applied directly. Ley 22.439 itself has no child-specific rule (its text contains no reference to minors). Practice: I found no readable primary source for this period. CELS's annual chapters for 2000–2002 on arbitrary detention and expulsion under the Ley Videla could not be opened (PDFs), so the rating is inferred.

In addition to the CRC (art. 75(22)), Ley 25.871 was in force from late January 2004. It added family reunification with minor children (arts. 3(d) and 10), the humanitarian and family-reunification waiver in art. 29, a higher fine for employing minors (art. 59), and school access regardless of status (art. 7). The law was not yet regulated. I found no readable practice evidence for around 2005, and CELS's 2005 chapter could not be opened.

New since 2005: Ley 26.061 (Nov 2005; arts. 1–3 make the CRC binding in every administrative decision), Ley 26.165 art. 53 (Dec 2006, protection of unaccompanied refugee minors), and Ley 26.364 art. 6 (May 2008, special procedures for child trafficking victims). Decreto 616/2010 did not take effect until July 2010. Practice: the CRC's 2010 concluding observations found stigmatisation of children from a migrant background and asked that migrant children be covered by the universal child allowance; CEDAW in 2010 noted gaps for unaccompanied asylum-seeking children.

Same framework, plus Decreto 616/2010 in force from July 2010 (art. 22(b) and art. 23(m) humanitarian residence; trafficking victims). DNU 70/2017 came later. Practice: the CMW in 2011 found discrimination against migrant children at school, and that the DNM did not weigh family circumstances before ordering expulsions. Nothing I read shows a later improvement before DNU 70/2017, so Rarely is kept.

answers.change_2000_2020: There have been right protections both in 2000 and 2020 but they are not the same

practice_sources.title: CELS: UN urges Argentina to derogate and suspend decree that violates migrant rights (CMW 2019)

answers.sourcing_note: Strong for the law: the original texts of Ley 25.871 and Decreto 616/2010, the child-protection, refugee and trafficking laws, and Ley 22.439 were all read. Practice evidence for 2000 and 2005 is missing: the CELS annual-report PDFs and the CRC 2002 observations could not be opened (no PDF reader available).
answers.notes: The 'Yes' on 1 January 2000 rests on the CRC, which has had constitutional rank since 1994 (art. 75(22)) and is treated as directly applicable; Ley 22.439 contained nothing child-specific. Later instruments added protections without removing any. DNU 70/2017 (Feb 2017 – March 2021) narrowed the art. 29 waiver and the expulsion safeguards; that history was not read, and it falls after 2015 in any case. Ley 26.842 (Dec 2012) amended Ley 26.364 but was not read.

answers_by_date.basis: CEDAW had constitutional rank under art. 75(22), and art. 75(23) mandates positive measures for women; these are the parts of the starting citation that were already in force. Ley 22.439 has no women-specific provision. Practice: I found no migrant-specific source for this period. CEDAW's 1997 observations (read) noted the lack of data on women held in slavery or exploited for prostitution. Rating inferred.
Added since 2000: art. 13 of Ley 25.871 (in force January 2004), which treats sex- or gender-based acts or omissions as discriminatory. No readable practice evidence for around 2005.

Added: Ley 26.165 arts. 42(f) and 53 (2006, specialised care for women asylum seekers who are victims of violence; UNHCR gender guidelines), Ley 26.364 art. 6 (2008, trafficking victims' rights, including to remain in the country), and Ley 26.485 (April 2009). Practice: CEDAW in 2010 recorded the State's own acknowledgment that migrant women's rights are not fully respected, and found gaps in protection for women asylum seekers. The CMW in 2011 found irregular migrant domestic workers exposed to sexual violence and exploitation, with limited access to remedies.

Added: Decreto 616/2010 art. 23(m)(3) (humanitarian residence for trafficking victims, in force July 2010). I found no documented improvement in practice after the 2010–2011 treaty-body findings; the CEDAW 2016 and CMW 2019 texts were not read.

answers.change_2000_2020: There have been right protections both in 2000 and 2020 but they are not the same

answers.sourcing_note: All statutes were read in their original texts, so the dating is solid. Practice evidence exists only around 2010–2011. The 1997 CEDAW findings are not specific to migrants, and the CEDAW 2016 and CMW 2019 texts could not be read.
answers.starting_answer_concern: The starting citation rests mainly on general instruments: CEDAW, art. 75(23), a non-discrimination clause (art. 13) and a general law on violence against women. The genuinely migrant-specific protections for women (Ley 26.165 arts. 42(f) and 53; trafficking-victim residence under Ley 26.364 art. 6 and Decreto 616/2010 art. 23(m)(3)) are not cited. Read strictly, the 2000 answer rests only on CEDAW and art. 75(23), which are close to the general principles the instrument says should not produce a Yes.
answers.notes: Yes is kept for 2000 and 2005 because the cited CEDAW and art. 75(23) were already in force. A stricter coder could answer No for those dates, since the migration-specific protections arrived only in 2006–2010.

answers_by_date.basis: Under Ley 22.439 there was no disability-specific protection: the text contains no reference to disability, incapacity or illness. Art. 75(23) of the Constitution is only a mandate to legislate. No practice evidence is needed.

Ley 25.871 (January 2004) added art. 10 (family reunification with adult children 'con capacidades diferentes') and art. 23(h) (residence extended to companions of disabled patients). The starting coder did not count these as the protection, so the answer stays No.
Same provisions as in 2005. Ley 26.378 (2008) approved the CRPD, but I did not read it. Decreto 616/2010 was not yet in force.

Decreto 616/2010 art. 20(c) (in force July 2010) gives migrants with disabilities, of any age, the same residence category as their parents, children or spouses. Like art. 10 and art. 23(h), it was in force on 1 January 2020 when the MRD coded No, so nothing changed between 2015 and 2020.

answers.change_2000_2020: There have been no right protections neither in 2000 nor in 2020

events.passage: c) Capacidades diferentes: A los extranjeros con capacidades diferentes, cualquiera fuera su edad, les corresponderá igual categoría de residencia que la otorgada a sus padres, hijos o cónyuges.

answers.repealed_search: I searched the text of Ley 22.439 for 'menor', 'incapac', 'discapac', 'enferm' and 'deficiencia' and found no disability protection. The list of norms amending Ley 22.439 shows only its regulations (Decretos 1434/87 and 1023/94) and fee and procedure acts. I could not open the text of Decreto 1023/94 (InfoLEG returned not found; the Refworld copy was blocked), so any provision it held is unverified. It was repealed by Decreto 616/2010, which replaced it with a more favourable rule (art. 20(c)). I found no protection that was repealed or narrowed before 2020.
answers.sourcing_note: Ley 22.439, Ley 25.871 (original text) and Decreto 616/2010 were read. Decreto 1023/94 and Ley 26.378 (CRPD) were not.
answers.starting_answer_concern: The 'No' looks doubtful on its own date. Art. 10 of Ley 25.871 guarantees family reunification with adult children with disabilities, art. 23(h) extends residence to companions of disabled patients, and Decreto 616/2010 art. 20(c) gives disabled migrants of any age their relatives' residence category. These are close to the instrument's Colombia example (beneficiary visa for disabled persons regardless of age), and suggest a Yes from 2004 (art. 10) or July 2010 (art. 20(c)) onward.
answers.notes: No is kept on every date because all the provisions that could support a Yes were already in force on 1 January 2020, when the MRD coded No. There is therefore no dated event between 2000 and 2020 that would change the answer within the starting coder's reading.
